editorNote: Graphical computing is leaving the laboratory and meeting the hard questions of software, speed and developer choice, while imaginative games stretch the home computer in other directions.
morningLine: This week in 1983: Lisa developers weigh their tools, M.U.L.E. and Suspended show new game ambitions, and Hurricane Alicia strikes Texas.

lead.headline: Apple Developers Confront the Lisa Software Puzzle
lead.dek: At Apple's August gathering, independent programmers see faster unreleased software—but face difficult choices about how to build for the graphical machine.
body: Apple's Lisa has made the graphical office a commercial proposition, but the machine's future now rests with people deciding what to make for it. At a week-long Independent Developers' Conference at the Dunfey Hotel in San Mateo, programmers gathered to compare methods, inspect works in progress and learn how Apple's unfamiliar visual environment might become a software market.

The contemporary Lisa newsletter Signal attended Lisa Day on August 11 and found developers choosing among standalone, windowed and Toolkit environments. The choice was not merely technical: it shaped how programs behaved, how closely they followed Lisa conventions and how much work their creators would assume. Signal reported that many developers still seemed unsure which route best suited their plans.

There was encouragement on the demonstration machines. Signal noted noticeable speed improvements in software not yet released, an important sign for a system often discussed as much for its deliberate pace as for its friendly interface. QuickDraw author Bill Atkinson also recalled Steve Jobs pressing for the rounded rectangles that helped give Lisa's display its distinctive, approachable character.

The opportunity remained expensive. Signal relayed a trade-paper claim that Apple's planned 1983 production of 20,000 Lisas was sold out, while sampled dealers quoted Lisa floppy media at $70 for five or $120 for ten. The conference revealed both sides of graphical computing's next step: remarkable tools and a developer community still working out how to turn them into fast, useful and affordable software.

stories.headline: Computer Games Grow Up: M.U.L.E. and Suspended Lead the Summer
stories.dek: Strategy, economics and interactive fiction claim feature space beside wargames and adventures.
body: The July-August Computer Gaming World treats two striking new designs as events worth extended attention. Electronic Arts' M.U.L.E. turns settlement and trade into a competitive economic contest, while Infocom's Suspended places the player inside a science-fiction crisis managed through remote senses and carefully chosen commands.

The same issue ranges through Battle for Normandy and adventure hints, evidence that computer gaming is no longer a single narrow genre. Its shelves now hold simulations, strategic contests and literary puzzles—experiences shaped as much by systems and imagination as by reflexes.

stories.headline: A $16.95 3-D Space Game Lands on Timex/Sinclair
stories.dek: Softsync's Mothership brings a pseudo-3-D corridor and two-player action to an entry-level computer.
body: The inexpensive Timex/Sinclair software economy has a new arcade entry. COMPUTE!'s August new-products pages list Softsync's Mothership at $16.95 plus $1.50 shipping and handling, a cassette-priced invitation to pilot Starlight Fighters through a hostile corridor.

The game offers one or two players, three difficulty levels, on-screen scoring and a pseudo-3-D display. Its keyboard becomes a control panel as players steer around drones—a compact example of publishers finding spectacle in machines built for a mass, budget-conscious audience.

stories.headline: IBM's ‘Peanut’ Rumor Keeps the Market Guessing
stories.dek: Expected low-cost and Unix machines stir speculation, but neither product has been announced.
body: The industry is already talking as though IBM's next personal computer has a nickname. Signal records expectations of a September unveiling for the rumored low-cost ‘Peanut,’ a machine whose shadow is influencing home-computer forecasts before IBM has formally introduced it.

The newsletter also relays an August Datamation report about ‘Popcorn,’ a rumored 68000-based Unix workstation near $10,000 and aimed at Lisa in 1984. Both remain period speculation, but the chatter shows competitors expecting IBM to press beyond the business desktop.
